comparison: Both address biochemical characterization of transgenic lines (C32-C37, C57). OpenEval finds the characterization comprehensive and sufficient. Peer reviewers request better explanation of homozygous vs hemizygous lines and justification for focusing on hemizygous lines, indicating uncertainty about the adequacy of characterization.

Both address predation data (C39-C43, C35-C36). Both evaluations agree that the data clearly demonstrate GLV-dependent differences in predator attraction and predation rates. OpenEval notes some marginally significant p-values but accepts the overall pattern; peer reviewers explicitly affirm these findings.

Both address fitness effects across years with different predator presence (C47-C51, C1, C48-C50). Both evaluations agree that the data demonstrate fitness benefits of GLVs when predators are present. Peer reviewers acknowledge this as 'a big step' in answering the fitness question.

Both address lack of TPI fitness benefits (C2, C44-C45). Both evaluations accept these findings. Peer reviewers commend the authors for reporting comprehensive measurements including those that don't fit hypotheses, indicating acceptance of the negative TPI results.

Both address TPI effects on larval behavior (C3, C53-C56). OpenEval finds the behavioral data well-supported across multiple assays. Peer reviewers question whether these experiments distract from the main narrative and suggest they could be omitted, indicating uncertainty about their relevance to the paper's conclusions.

Both address the main conclusion about GLV fitness benefits (C1). OpenEval finds it well-supported by the matched plant experiments. Peer reviewers also accept this finding, acknowledging it as a significant contribution to understanding indirect defense fitness effects.

Both address the 2010 control year data (C47). OpenEval views it as a critical negative control. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this finding as it supports the predator-dependent fitness effect they explicitly affirm.

Both address reduced herbivore damage on GLV-deficient plants (C46). OpenEval notes this strengthens the conclusion that TPIs don't function as direct defenses. Peer reviewers commend reporting of findings that don't fit hypotheses, indicating acceptance.

Both address the inference that TPIs increase predation susceptibility (C4). OpenEval finds this lacks direct validation and notes contradictory trends. Peer reviewers' suggestion to potentially omit the TPI behavioral experiments indicates similar uncertainty about this inference.

Both address GLV conversion by Manduca oral secretions (C25). OpenEval accepts this as citation-supported background. Peer reviewers accept the claim but request a technical terminology correction (rearrangement vs isomerization), indicating acceptance of the underlying science.
OpenEval evaluates justification for using buds/flowers as fitness proxies (C59-C64). No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though this methodological choice was not challenged by reviewers.
OpenEval evaluates scientific context and rationale claims (C5-C12). No corresponding peer review evaluation found; these background claims were not specifically addressed by reviewers.

OpenEval evaluates TPI background and slow growth-high mortality hypothesis (C13-C18). No corresponding peer review evaluation found; these theoretical framework claims were not specifically addressed by reviewers.
OpenEval evaluates control experiments and system characterization (C38, C52, C70-C76). No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though these controls were not challenged by reviewers.
OpenEval evaluates hemi-irLOX2 characterization showing WT TPI levels (C57-C58). While C57 overlaps with R5, the specific mechanistic explanation in C58 was not addressed by peer reviewers.
OpenEval evaluates speculative applications and future directions (C65-C69). No corresponding peer review evaluation found; these discussion points were not specifically addressed by reviewers.
